video_title: More & More Signals Popping Up That Suggest A Pullback Is Near | Lance Roberts
gist: Lance Roberts and Adam Taggart's weekly recap: NVIDIA's blowout quarter (revenue $96B, +106% YoY) is real growth unlike the dot-com era, but Roberts runs an underweight 4% position and plans to rotate to hyperscalers once the ~18-24 month data-center buildout matures. He reads Kevin Warsh's Jackson Hole speech as signaling no September hike but a possible year-end one, flags a hedge-fund basis trade distorting the bond-market rate signal, and argues the economy is two-sided: data-center capex (a rare burst of productive investment) is masking real demand destruction (Chicago PMI 58.3→47.1, payrolls revised -79k) that disinflationary forces will eventually win. Technically he's cautious short-term with a risk-reduction signal possibly within 2-3 weeks, targeting a pullback toward the 50-day MA before a year-end rally.

insights.claim: NVIDIA's quarter showed revenue up 106% YoY to $96B, data-center revenue $89B (+117%), operating income $63.7B (+124%), 75% gross margins and non-GAAP EPS of $2.22 (+122%), with the growth 'real' unlike dot-com-era Global Crossing/Lucent, though rising accounts receivable is a genuine concern if end customers fail to pay.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Watch NVIDIA's accounts-receivable trend as the tell on vendor-financed demand; Roberts' base case is real revenue so any AI 'ding' won't be a dot-com-scale crisis.
insights.quote: if you would just assume that a 100% of their accounts receivables are never going to get paid well you know then that's certainly worth being careful about

insights.claim: Roberts holds NVIDIA at only ~4% portfolio weight, deliberately underweight versus its S&P 500 benchmark allocation, staying in the trade for the buildout but sizing for the risk.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: A concrete positioning template: participate in the AI-infra buildout but stay underweight the single most-crowded name rather than avoid or overweight it.
insights.quote: we carry right now about a 4% weight in Nvidia, which is underneath we're underweight Nvidia relative to what our allocation would be otherwise

insights.claim: NVIDIA's ~100% earnings growth is unsustainable by the law of large numbers, and within 1-2 years the data-center buildout ('building the factory') ends and revenue shifts to the hyperscalers operating those centers, at which point Roberts will rotate portfolio weight toward Microsoft, Amazon and Google.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: The actionable rotation call: as buildout capex peaks in the next 1-2 years, the beneficiary shifts from the chip supplier to the hyperscalers monetizing data-center operation.
insights.quote: when we start to see that switch then we'll switch our holdings in our portfolios more towards the hyperscalers

themes.theme: Fed policy & Warsh at Jackson Hole

insights.claim: Kevin Warsh's Jackson Hole speech argued financial conditions are not restrictive at all (capex +9%, S&P profits +20%, credit spreads near cycle lows, banks easing lending standards, stocks near highs, low volatility), holding the 2% inflation target and giving himself room to hike if needed while pushing markets to stop relying on the Fed for direction.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Warsh framing policy as non-restrictive keeps a hike optionality alive; the takeaway is markets must reprice away from expecting Fed support, with gold/silver/bitcoin selling off on the reduced-liquidity read.
insights.quote: from his view, policy is not restrictive at all. And gives him a little bit of wiggle room that if he needed to hike rates some, he could.

insights.claim: Roberts expects no Fed hike in September but a possible hike by year-end, aligning with Darius Dale's view that the Fed 'flexes' short-term (possibly one hike or 50bps by year-end) to set up a subsequent easing campaign.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Positions the near-term rate path as hawkish-then-dovish: a possible year-end hike precedes easing, a sequence to trade rate-sensitive assets around.

insights.claim: About 50 hedge funds own ~8.5% of the bond market via a heavily-leveraged (10x) basis trade, shorting bonds to push near-term rates up and distorting the Treasury-yield signal by inflating the term premium above fundamentals; Bessent's Treasury buyback operation (Sept 4-9) aims to compress that term premium, creating friction with Warsh's desire for a clean market signal.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: The current Treasury-yield signal is technically distorted by the basis trade, so rates may overstate fundamental growth/inflation; the Bessent-Warsh tension over intervention is a policy risk to monitor.
insights.quote: 50 hedge funds own roughly about eight and a half% of the bond market... They've got 10 times leverage in this fun in these types of trades.

insights.claim: Today's interest rates only seem high because 2008-present ZIRP and QE artificially suppressed them; rates are simply normalizing, and returning them toward 2022 levels would clip roughly $500B off federal interest spending.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Reframes 'high' rates as normalization, not restriction; the $500B interest-savings figure links lower rates directly to fiscal relief, though Roberts doubts politicians would actually cut spending.
insights.quote: from 2008 to present, we had zero interest rates and massive quantities of QE. And so the interest rate was being suppressed artificially. Now it's returned back to normal levels.

themes.theme: Two-sided economy: capex boom vs demand destruction

insights.claim: The economy is bifurcated: the data-center buildout drives a strong business-investment side (economic composite index rose from ~30 to ~40 in months) while employment and incomes weaken, evidenced by Chicago PMI falling from 58.3 to 47.1 and a -79,000 non-farm payroll benchmark revision against Goldman's expected +50k-to-450k.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Headline growth (~1.5%) masks underlying labor weakness; a negative payroll revision plus collapsing Chicago PMI are early signs demand destruction is building beneath the capex-driven surface.
insights.quote: That revision came in at a negative 79,000. So we actually despite the fact we've had a whole slate of weak employment numbers since the beginning of this year it was actually 79,000 jobs worse

insights.claim: The AI buildout represents the first major productive investment since the 1950s, raising productivity and driving onshoring (inflationary, temporary), but this masks demand destruction from high oil (Iran), tariffs and higher rates that will persist another 18-24 months before long-term disinflationary forces (demographics, debt) win out.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Sets a ~18-24 month clock: inflationary capex tailwinds fade and structural disinflation (demographics/debt) reasserts, favoring a long-duration disinflation thesis once the buildout matures.
insights.quote: The long-term effects of debts and deficits are disinflationary. And we're going to get back into that cycle at some point.

insights.claim: Statistically, a positive August in a year where the market is already up more than 10% has been followed by a decent return through year-end about 91% of the time, supporting momentum despite short-term caution.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: A seasonality edge: the up-August/up-10% setup historically favors a year-end rally, tempering near-term bearishness.
insights.quote: when you have a positive August and a year where the market is up more than 10% about 91% of the time you've had a decent return through the end of this year

insights.claim: Roberts is short-term cautious with a live sell signal and weakening momentum, advising stops near the previous highs / 50-day moving average and expecting a possible pullback to the 50-day, while sharing Mark Newton's view of choppiness into the midterms then an S&P rally toward 8,000 by year-end.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Concrete risk-management levels: use the 50-day MA / prior highs as stops and expect chop-then-rally into a ~8,000 year-end S&P target.
insights.quote: from a riskmanagement standpoint, I would have stops kind of set around the previous highs, maybe around the 50-day moving average.

insights.claim: Market breadth is still broad (bullish) but functions as a contrarian signal once too many stocks sit above their 200-day MA (~70-75%); Roberts expects any risk-reduction signal from his breadth/money-flow indicators within the next 2-3 weeks, implying a 3-5% (up to 10%) correction before the next buy signal.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: The near-term timing tell: a reversal in breadth/money-flow within 2-3 weeks would be the trigger to raise cash ahead of a modest correction, not a crash.
insights.quote: if there's going to be a risk reduction signal, it'll be within the next two to three weeks.

insights.claim: The US is reported close to a ~100-year lease deal to operate a number of Venezuela's oil fields, which would roughly double US proven oil reserves and see Venezuela leave OPEC (after the UAE already left), removing US dependence on OPEC pricing and the Strait of Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: A doubling of US reserves plus OPEC fracturing would cement US energy security and pricing leverage; watch for OPEC destabilization and oil-major capex into Venezuelan fields if the lease closes.
insights.quote: it it is being reported that the US is very close... to striking a long-term like 100-year lease deal with Venezuela... which they're saying would essentially double the US proven oil reserves
